newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Thousands mourn victims of suspected Dutch arson.
newsitem.headline: Thousands mourn victims of suspected Dutch arson.

text.p: Thousands of mourners wept and prayed in a Hague square on Friday over the coffins of six victims of what Dutch media said may have been a racist arson attack.
A Turkish woman and five of her children died in a fire at their home in the city on Tuesday night. Her husband and the couple's five other children escaped by jumping from an upstairs window.

The Hague's mayor told relatives of the victims that the fire had apparently been deliberately set, reports said, although he emphasised in a television interview that it was still unclear who was responsible or what their motives were.
The coffins, draped with Turkish flags, were carried through an emotional crowd of about 2,500 in the Jacob van Kampen square after a memorial service at a mosque. Many kissed them as they passed.

The coffins were loaded into hearses to be driven in procession to Amsterdam's Schipol airport and flown to Turkey for burial. A silent "March of Grief and Despair" was being held in The Hague later on Friday, led by the mayor.

On the night that the victims died buildings in the same area housing an Azerbaijani-Turkish centre and a Turkish islamic association were attacked with petrol bombs, but police have refused to comment on any possible link between the incidents.
Five men arrested on Thursday over the petrol bomb attacks have now been released and are not suspects in the deadly house fire, the Hague public prosecutor said on Friday.
"These persons are not suspected of arson in the house," the prosecutor's office said in a statement.

"(They)...were held on suspicion of throwing molotov cocktails at two cultural centres/coffeehouses in the area. The prosecutor has decided to let (them) go, because they all have a firm alibi and could not have been involved."

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo has sent a letter of condolence to the Turkish ambassador expressing his sympathy to bereaved relatives and his dismay that the fire appeared to have been intentionally started, the Foreign Ministry said.

"I was sleeping and I heard a noise like an exploding bomb, a huge bomb," the father of the family told Dutch television. "When I opened the passage door the flames hit me. I couldn't get to my children."
Prime Minister Wim Kok said that even the suspicion of a racist attack was worrying for the Netherlands, which prides itself on the tolerance of its society.
"The thought that we could be dealing with arson with some ethnic intention is dramatic," he said. "That would be an entirely new phenomenon in the Netherlands and a serious signal."
Some in the Turkish community were less sure that a racist attack would be an isolated incident.
"It gets media attention only if it involves more than just a fire," a local Turkish journalist told the Dutch ANP news agency.
"In recent times there have been fairly regular, if not successful, attacks on immigrant targets."
